analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal housing loans for manufactured home communities on basic tenant protections like rent-increase notice and sale rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 27, 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee the same day; the committee has taken no further action, and the bill has not received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require owners of manufactured home communities to give residents basic protections in order to get federally backed loans to build, rehabilitate, or buy communities. Those protections include one-year renewable leases, 60-day written notice of rent increases with a written justification, a 60-day heads-up before a community is sold or closed, and the right for residents to sell their homes without moving them out of the park. It would also set money penalties for owners who break the rules and create a commission to propose stronger standards later.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities, most of whom own their homes but rent the land underneath them. They gain lease stability, advance notice of rent hikes and closures, the right to sell their home in place, and cash penalties when owners violate the rules. Because the conditions attach to any community owned by a loan borrower or that borrower's affiliates, the protections reach beyond just the financed property.

how_it_helps.text: Requires one-year lease terms renewable unless the owner has good cause for non-renewal, ending the practice of non-renewing tenants without reason.

Requires at least 60 days' written notice of any rent increase or new charge, with a written justification of operating costs; increases above 5% require an extra 30 days' notice for each additional 2.5% increase.
Requires 60 days' advance written notice before a community is sold or closed, with a 60-day window in which the owner must negotiate in good faith if residents want to buy the community.

Gives tenants a 5-day grace period on rent, a 15-day right to cure a default, the right to post a 'For Sale' sign, and the right to sell their home in place without relocating it, including for at least 45 days after an eviction.

Sets money penalties for violations, including repayment of illegal charges plus 25% with interest, six months' rent for wrongful termination, and a two-year ban on future federal financing for willful violators.
Applies the conditions to any community owned by the loan borrower or the borrower's affiliates, so owners cannot protect only the financed property while raising rents elsewhere.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of manufactured home communities, many of them large corporate investors, would bear the cost of lease restrictions, notice requirements, penalty payments, and the risk of losing access to federally backed financing. Lenders would lose a pool of eligible loans. Owners could try to pass some costs to residents through higher base rents before the protections kick in.

drawbacks.text: The protections only bind owners who take federally backed financing; communities financed outside HUD, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac programs would not be covered.

Conditioning federal financing on tenant protections could shrink the pool of eligible loans, making it harder for some owners to borrow to buy or improve communities; the bill offsets this somewhat by requiring a standard lease so that home-mortgage lending in compliant communities stays workable.

Compliance, documentation, and penalty costs fall on owners and could be passed to residents through higher base rents or reduced services, though the notice-and-justification rules make abrupt shifts harder.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents — who typically own their home but not the land and can rarely afford to move it — the protections address the core vulnerability of the arrangement: a landlord who controls the lot can raise rent sharply or close the park, and the home is effectively stranded. The main costs fall on owners and lenders, and the strongest honest objection is the risk of reduced lending and possible pass-through of compliance costs. On balance the bill trades a modest, conditional restriction on financing for significant security for a group with little market power.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since, so it has not come anywhere near a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Brittany Pettersen introduced the bill in the House on March 27, 2025, joined by Reps. Bonamici, Larson of Connecticut, and Tlaib.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote since the referral; the bill remains with the committee while Congress is still in session.
The bill has 6 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, owners of manufactured home communities and the investors behind them, because no federal financing conditions have taken effect and residents remain without the proposed protections.

for.name: Rep. Brittany Pettersen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought its original cosponsors on board.

for.name: Reps. Suzanne Bonamici, John Larson, and Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. French Hill (R-AR)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has held no hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All listed sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the opposing party with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors
industries.note: The bill conditions federally backed financing on lease protections, rent-increase justification, closure notice, and penalty payments. Many communities are owned by large investors that profit by raising lot rents on residents who own their homes but cannot afford to move them, so the industry's interest runs against the residents the bill protects.

industries.industry: Lenders and mortgage investors in manufactured home community loans
industries.note: Noncompliant loans could no longer be insured by HUD or purchased by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, shrinking the pool of eligible lending. At the same time, the bill's standard lease provision is designed to keep mortgage lending in compliant communities workable.

The mortgage giants would be barred from buying noncompliant community loans and would take on new duties: publishing covered properties, helping develop a standard site lease, and joining a standards commission. The conditions reduce their risk from loans to owners who raise rents on captive residents.

analysis.trajectory: A first-year bill with a small, Democratic-only cosponsor list sitting in a committee controlled by the other party usually goes nowhere; it would need to attract Republican support or ride along with a larger housing package to get a hearing, let alone a vote, before this Congress ends in January 2027.
